q-132255:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the constant multiple and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y{z}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y{z}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(y{z}^{2})}^{2}}})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}{z}^{4}}})\cdot y\cdot 2z \\  & =-\frac{2yz\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}{z}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,\frac{1}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}{|}_{(3,\,1/2,\,1)} & =-\frac{2(\frac{1}{2})(1)\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}(1)^{4}}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

q-35715:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the constant multiple and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(xy)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(xy)^{2}}}\cdot (x) \\  & =\frac{xz}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-109084:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX+b]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\sqrt{3}$ and $b=-5.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{3}X-5] & ={(\sqrt{3})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

q-129390:
Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}X] & ={(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{2}{4}\cdot 10 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

q-109226:
First, let's find $\text{E}[X].$ 

The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.74+1\cdot 0.07+2\cdot 0.08+3\cdot 0.09+4\cdot 0.02 \\  & =0.58.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[0.5X] & =0.5\text{E}[X] \\  & =0.5\cdot 0.58 \\  & =0.29.\end{aligned}
$$

q-109234:
For any constants $a$ and $b$ and any random variable $X,$ we have

$$
\text{E}[aX+b]=a\text{E}[X]+b.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[-6X-1] & =-6\text{E}[X]-1 \\  & =-6(-\frac{3}{2})-1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36623:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is not defined when $y=0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{y})) \\  & =\frac{-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}}{1+{(\frac{x}{y})}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ is not defined at the point $(0,0).$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-132639:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when 

$$
\begin{aligned}z & >0\,\text{and}\,x+y\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(z)}{x+y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{1}{z} \\  & =\frac{1}{z(x+y)}\end{aligned}
$$

The function ${f}_{z}(x,y,z)$ is defined only for 

$$
\begin{aligned}z(x+y) & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the domain of ${f}_{z}$ is

$$
{D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $z$ exists on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,z\ne 0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,z>0\,\,\text{and}\,\,x+y\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-132655:
First, notice that $f(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{-x}}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y)=-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-65252:
First, notice that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ is defined only when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y)=1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ is defined only when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.
$$

- The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-132732:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡z} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{sin}⁡z} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{{sin}^{2}⁡z}) \\  & =-\frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{x{sin}^{2}⁡z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is false. If we substitute $(0,1,\frac{\pi }{2})$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(0,1,\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ into $f$, we get

$$
f(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡0}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4})$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4})=\frac{1}{(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}=\sqrt{2},
$$

and ${f}_{z}$ is also defined at $(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{z}(1,1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-\frac{(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}{(1){sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}=-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'III only'.

q-72011:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-y}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}}{2\sqrt{x-y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}\cdot \frac{-1}{2\sqrt{x-y}} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{x-y}}}{2\sqrt{x-y}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,-1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,-1)={e}^{\sqrt{1-(-1)}}={e}^{\sqrt{2}},
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1)=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1-(-1)}}}{2\sqrt{1-(-1)}}=-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{2}}}{2\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,0)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,0)={e}^{\sqrt{1-0}}={e}^{1}=e,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,0) & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1-0}}}{2\sqrt{1-0}}=\frac{{e}^{1}}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{e}{2} \\ {f}_{y}(1,0) & =-\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1-0}}}{2\sqrt{1-0}}=-\frac{{e}^{1}}{2\sqrt{1}}=-\frac{e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(1,1)=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{1-1}}}{2\sqrt{1-1}}=\frac{{e}^{0}}{2\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0}
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II  only'.

q-80400:
To find $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{∂f}{∂y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(1+3xy)) \\  & =3{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(1+3xy)+3x{y}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1+3xy)\end{aligned}
$$

q-65065:
To find $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{∂f}{∂y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{3{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{6y({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})-3{y}^{2}(3{y}^{2})}{{({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6y{x}^{3}+6{y}^{4}-9{y}^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6y{x}^{3}-3{y}^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3y(2{x}^{3}-{y}^{3})}{{({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-80473:
To find ${g}_{xx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({g}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{2}{2x-y}) \\  & =-\frac{4}{(2x-y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${g}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({g}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\frac{1}{2x-y}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{(2x-y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we evaluate ${g}_{xx}(x,y)$ and ${g}_{yy}(x,y)$ at $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{xx}(1,-1) & =-\frac{4}{(2(1)-(-1))^{2}}=-\frac{4}{9} \\ {g}_{yy}(1,-1) & =-\frac{1}{(2(1)-(-1))^{2}}=-\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
{g}_{xx}(1,-1)+{g}_{yy}(1,-1)=-\frac{4}{9}-\frac{1}{9}=-\frac{5}{9}.
$$

q-80468:
To find ${f}_{xy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})) \\  & =x\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot (-2y)) \\  & =2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

To find ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})) \\  & =-y(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot 2x) \\  & =2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y)+{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})+2xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =4xy\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
